title: Exploring the Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Thematic Analysis
extended_summary:
This paper examines how educators perceive the benefits, risks, and pedagogical implications of generative AI in education, with a particular focus on tools such as ChatGPT, Bard, and Bing AI. The central question is not an intervention study but a thematic exploration of educator viewpoints on how GenAI affects learning, assessment, academic integrity, prompt construction, programming support, and responsible use. The authors aim to surface both opportunities and concerns, especially around plagiarism, hallucinated outputs, over-reliance, bias, transparency, and the need for updated assessment practices.

The study is based on seven unstructured essays written by education-sector professionals, all of whom taught in higher education contexts across subjects such as machine learning, programming, databases, statistics, and research methods. The paper combines thematic analysis with exploratory data analysis of the essays, including word-frequency and bigram analyses. The educators discuss GenAI as a tool for boilerplate code generation, troubleshooting, iterative prompting, and personalized support, while also warning about misuse, inaccurate outputs, weak arithmetic performance, and the erosion of independent thinking.

The main conclusions are that educators see GenAI as both promising and risky, and that effective use depends heavily on prompt quality, human oversight, and curricular guidance. The most prominent concern is academic integrity, with strong emphasis on replacing traditional essay-heavy assessment with more authentic forms of evaluation such as oral questioning, project-based work, and monitored interaction. The paper also argues that students and staff need explicit instruction on responsible GenAI use, and that institutions should develop clearer policies, better assessment designs, and more transparent practices for integrating these tools into teaching and learning.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI / large language model system for text generation, question answering, coding help, and other prompt-based outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as a generative AI tool used by students and educators for coding help, simulated data generation, essay writing, troubleshooting, and as a general education example; also referenced in relation to prompts, hallucinations, arithmetic errors, and assessment misuse.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's conversational generative AI / large language model system for text generation and question answering.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned via the prior name Bard and discussed as an example of generative AI in education, including differences from ChatGPT and use in writing/response generation.

identified_tools.name: Turnitin
identified_tools.description: An originality/similarity detection system used to compare submitted text against existing sources and produce a similarity score.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the example originality detector to explain how similarity scoring works, and to argue that such tools can be misinterpreted as definitive plagiarism detectors.

identified_tools.name: GPTZero
identified_tools.description: A product claiming to detect whether text was generated by AI or written by humans.
identified_tools.use_case: Cited as an example of an LLM-generated-content detector discussed in terms of claimed accuracy and limitations.

identified_tools.name: ZeroGPT
identified_tools.description: A product claiming to detect AI-generated text versus human-written text.
identified_tools.use_case: Cited alongside GPTZero as an example of AI-content detection software and its limitations.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative thematic analysis of educator opinions rather than an empirical evaluation of a tool. It discusses mechanisms, concerns, and examples, but reports no experimental outcome data or effect sizes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical implications for how generative AI and detection tools are used in education, especially around assessment and academic integrity, but it does not measure impact on learner outcomes. The influence is therefore suggestive but unquantified.
